analysis.one_liner: Requires annual public reports on whether offshore oil wells, platforms, and pipelines are being decommissioned as required.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with three Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Energy Committee, which held a subcommittee hearing in July 2026 but has taken no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires companies to plug offshore oil and gas wells and remove platforms and pipelines when they are done with them. This bill would require the Interior Department to publish a yearly report showing how often that actually happens: how many decommissioning applications came in, how many wells and pipelines missed their deadlines, how many got permission to be left in place instead of removed, and what enforcement actions the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement took. The report would go to Congress and be posted publicly online.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people get a clearer picture of whether oil companies are plugging and removing offshore infrastructure on schedule, or leaving behind wells and pipelines that can leak and whose cleanup costs can fall on taxpayers. Congress and the public also gain an annual record of enforcement, including civil penalties and companies barred from future offshore work.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Secretary to submit and publicly post an annual report covering decommissioning applications received, infrastructure that missed its legally required decommissioning deadline, and wells, platforms, and pipelines approved to be decommissioned in place rather than removed [S2].

The report must also include the status of enforcement actions by the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement, such as notices of noncompliance, civil penalties, and disqualifications from future offshore operations, giving the public a running record of whether violations are being punished [S2].

The report must break out the length of offshore pipelines that were decommissioned in place versus actually removed, focusing attention on how much abandoned infrastructure remains on the seabed [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas operators would face additional public scrutiny of their decommissioning records and the Interior Department would take on the administrative work of compiling the annual report. The bill imposes no new fees, plugging requirements, or penalties.

drawbacks.text: The bill is transparency-only: it requires no additional plugging, no new penalties, and no cleanup funding, so even if the reports reveal widespread missed decommissioning deadlines, nothing in the bill forces the problem to be fixed [S2].
The first report would not be due until two years after enactment, so the public would wait a considerable time for the first picture of compliance [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's cost is minimal and its value is real but limited: it creates a public annual record of how well the existing decommissioning rules are being followed, which is a precondition for Congress ever acting on the issue, but it does not itself plug a single well or fund any cleanup. A person wanting offshore wells actually plugged on schedule would see this as a first step, not a fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee for a hearing in July 2026, but the committee has not voted on it or sent it to the full Senate, and the session has not ended.

narrative.text: Senator Peter Welch introduced the bill on March 26, 2026, joined by Senators Merkley, Wyden, and Markey [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S4].
On July 15, 2026, the committee's Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining held a hearing on the bill [S4].
No further action — no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the action history, and the 119th Congress remains in session [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has clearly gained or lost. Offshore operators face no new requirements while the bill sits in committee, and the public still has no annual decommissioning report.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, neither side; bill still sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the report requirement on offshore decommissioning.

for.name: 3 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Merkley, Wyden, and Markey).

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral, sending it only to a subcommittee hearing without scheduling a committee vote or floor action.

sides.party_line_note: There has been no vote, so no roll-call exists; all four sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, but no one has publicly opposed it either.

industries.note: The bill imposes no new obligations but would publicly expose each year how often companies miss decommissioning deadlines and what penalties they face, creating reputational and enforcement-oversight risk for an industry whose savings from skipped plugging can become public cleanup and pollution costs.

industries.industry: Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement / Interior Department
industries.note: The department would carry the annual reporting workload, but the bill also gives its enforcement record a public showcase, which could support demands for more staff and authority.

analysis.trajectory: With a hearing already held, the bill has passed the earliest subcommittee stage, but bills that stop there rarely advance. In a Senate controlled by the other party with no Republican cosponsors, the realistic path from here is that the committee never votes on it and the bill dies at the end of the session unless a broader energy or ocean bill picks up its language.
